name: Yace
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: OLAC listing for Yace [ekr] (language-archives.org, Internet Archive copy 2022-12-06) and Glottolog 5.3 bibliography for yace1238 (4 entries: Armstrong 1981, Watson 1930, Armstrong 1955, Stahlke 1970)
sources.note: Bibliographic check only: no grammar, grammar sketch or phonology of Yace is registered in either catalogue; OLAC lists no language descriptions beyond Glottolog/Ethnologue records.

sources.citation: Olawe, Opeyemi Emmanuel. 2022. A parametric variation of English and Ekpari inflection system. International Journal of Language, Linguistics, Literature and Culture 1(2): 48-62. doi:10.59009/ijlllc.2022.0010
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone (data untonemarked). Contrastive inflectional morphology of Ekpari (Yace), 'Akpa dialect spoken among the Alifokpa clan'; p.51 states that little or no study has explored Ekpari morphology, syntax, phonology or semantics.

sources.citation: Otronyi, Linus & John Muniru. 2017. Is Yace a dialect of Yala? Paper presented at the Conference of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria, Port Harcourt, December 2017. SIL Nigeria. HAL hal-01998021.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. Sociolinguistic survey (Aug 2017) with wordlist comparison showing Yace is a distinct language from Yala; sec. 1.1 'Previous research' lists only Armstrong 1981b (wordlist), Stahlke 1970, Armstrong 1989 and Udoh 2003 for Yace; 1980 Gospel of Mark is the only printed vernacular material.

sources.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. 1983. The Idomoid languages of the Benue and Cross River valleys. Journal of West African Languages 13(1): 91-149. (open scan from journalofwestafricanlanguages.org; no text layer; read via page images and the scanned text already
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress anywhere. p.96: Igede has a four-level register tone system; 'All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems. Except for the very special case of Yala (Ikom), downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent.' Yatye (Ekpari, Alifokpa) is listed as an Idomoid language grouped with Akweya/Akpa but 'only referred to occasionally in this study' (p.139); the per-language phonology charts cover Idoma dialects, Eloyi, Igede, Etulo and Akweya, not Yatye.

sources.citation: Stahlke, Herbert F. W. 1976. Segment sequences and segmental fusion. Studies in African Linguistics 7(1): 41-63. (open, full-issue PDF)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or on the tone system; sec. 3.2 'Voiceless nasals in Yatye' treats verb+noun contraction and nasal fusion; fn. 9, 11 identify Yatye (c. 20,000 speakers) and its dialects (Alifokpa vs others).

sources.citation: Stahlke, Herbert F. W. 1970. Serial verbs. Studies in African Linguistics 1(1): 60-99. (open, full-issue PDF from journals.flvc.org)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Yatye data (own fieldwork 1965-67, Alifokpa area) transcribed with three tones: p.60 fn.1 gives high/low/mid tone-marking conventions; p.80 states the Yatye perfect is marked by a mid tone on all verb prefixes in a series and the imperfect by a low-high tone sequence (grammatical tone).

sources.note: Phonology of Akpa/Akweya [akf], the sister language Armstrong pairs with Yatye as one 'Akweya-Yatye language'; the nearest thing to a phonological study in the Yatye-Akpa branch and may comment on Yatye prosody in passing (would be an Akpa, not Yace, statement).
